:::{#exm-arithmetic-code}
#### An arithmetic code for a short message

<!-- no-figure: the example is a table of intervals and one codeword -->

Take a source with the values $a$, $b$ and $c$, in that order,
and the probabilities $(0.5, 0.3, 0.2)$.
The code below follows the steps of @def-arithmetic-code for the message $a, c, b, a$.
It prints the interval after each step,
then the codeword and the codeword length.

```{r}
#| label: arithmetic-code
p <- c(a = 0.5, b = 0.3, c = 0.2)
cdf_before <- cumsum(p) - p
message_values <- c("a", "c", "b", "a")
n <- length(message_values)
lower <- 0
width <- 1
lowers <- numeric(n)
widths <- numeric(n)
for (i in seq_len(n)) {
  symbol <- message_values[i]
  lower <- lower + width * cdf_before[[symbol]]
  width <- width * p[[symbol]]
  lowers[i] <- lower
  widths[i] <- width
}
data.frame(symbol = message_values, lower = lowers, upper = lowers + widths, width = widths)
midpoint <- lower + width / 2
surprisal <- -log2(width)
n_digits <- ceiling(surprisal) + 1
positions <- seq_len(n_digits)
digits <- floor(midpoint * 2^positions) %% 2
codeword <- paste0(digits, collapse = "")
c(midpoint = midpoint, codeword_length = n_digits, surprisal = surprisal)
codeword
```

The final interval has width $`r width`$,
which is the product $0.5 \times 0.2 \times 0.3 \times 0.5$ of the probabilities of the four values.
The codeword is $`r codeword`$,
with $`r n_digits`$ digits,
which is the message's [surprisal](entropy.qmd#def-surprisal) of $`r round(surprisal, 3)`$ bits rounded up to a whole number,
plus one.

:::
